suggestions:
- Implement an explicit save consent flow: before persisting UNAME/pc-info, show a concise preview of fields to be stored (hostname, OS, kernel, arch, CPU, RAM, disks, GPU, BIOS, motherboard) and require explicit confirmation. Allow partial saves if only some fields are ready.

- Harden redaction with a configurable policy: auto-mask sensitive identifiers (serials, MACs, UUIDs, license keys) by default across all outputs and exports; provide per-field redaction controls and an option to reveal only with explicit override.

- Encrypt and log memory persistence: store the persistent PC memory encrypted at rest with a master key; maintain an immutable audit log (timestamp, action, fields saved) to detect tampering or unauthorized changes.

- Improve tool-missing fallbacks and guidance: if a required tool (e.g., dmidecode, lscpu) is missing, auto-suggest/install steps or gracefully skip that data with a clear annotation, rather than blocking the workflow.

- Standardize data model and user feedback: use a defined pc-info schema (OS/name, CPU model/cores, RAM, disks/partitions, GPU/driver, motherboard, BIOS, hostname); after each save, display a brief diff against the previous snapshot and indicate any omissions or redactions.

- Enforce a default redaction policy with explicit per-field control: auto-redact serials, MACs, UUIDs on every save by default, but expose a CLI/config flag (and per-field toggles) to disable or selectively enable redaction. Ensure redaction is applied before any persistence or log output.

- Add a data-preview step before saving: show a concise summary of what will be stored (OS fields, CPU model/cores, RAM, disks, GPU, etc.) with redaction masks visible, and require user confirmation to proceed.

- Use a versioned, encrypted persistent memory store: store PC info in a schema with versioning, encrypt at rest, and include basic integrity checks and migration notes for future schema changes.

- Streamline the “next step” UX with a deterministic default: present a single recommended action (e.g., “Save LSCPU snapshot now”) plus clear alternatives (MEMORY/DISKS/DMIDECODE or run pc-info), with a one-tap path to proceed.

- Improve resume/recovery behavior: persist an explicit session state/token and provide a dedicated resume/continue command, automatically detecting partial captures (e.g., LSCPU only) and guiding the user to complete the remaining sections.

- Implement a persistent redaction policy with clear opt-in: add a configurable mode (enabled/disabled/ask-per-save), plus a dry-run preview of what would be redacted before saving, with per-user config storage.

- Add a single, versioned save command: persist all collected data (OS/UNAME, LSCPU, MEMORY, DISKS, DMIDECODE) to an encrypted, auditable store with timestamp, changelog, and optional automatic backups; support selective saving if needed.

- Make parsing/merging idempotent: when new partial data arrives (e.g., only Socket(s) from LSCPU), merge into existing state instead of overwriting; surface and resolve any data conflicts or ambiguities.

- Improve guidance and flow: propose a default path (save CPU snapshot now with redaction, then paste rest or run pc-info all); provide a concise summary of what will be saved before confirmation.

- Strengthen validation and consistency checks: verify cross-field consistency (e.g., architecture/CPU family between LSCPU and OS data), flag discrepancies, and block saves until resolved or clearly explain actions to take.

- Add a pre-save redaction preview and make redaction opt-in by default with per-field policy: automatically redact serials, MACs, UUIDs, etc., show a preview of the redacted output before saving, and allow easy toggling via config.

- Harden LSCPU parsing with validation and normalization: detect and fix inconsistencies (e.g., L3 cache count vs. CPUs), consolidate per-field summaries (L1d/L1i/L2/L3 with counts), and store a canonical, unit-consistent snapshot.

- Introduce versioned snapshots and diffs: save each snapshot with a version/timestamp, provide a diff against the previous version, and support rollback to earlier versions if needed.

- Implement persistent-memory autosave with config-driven path: allow enabling/disabling autosave to a designated path (e.g., JSON/YAML file), ensure atomic writes, and provide a clear status indicator in the CLI.

- Improve prompts and defaults: present a concise, actionable default (e.g., “Save LSCPU with redaction (Y/n)?”), clearly list what will be saved, and require explicit confirmation to avoid ambiguous actions.

- Add configurable redaction with per-field rules and a preview before saving: auto-redact serials/MACs/UUIDs, with a user-tacit option to save redacted or unredacted copies.

- Standardize output formats (JSON/YAML) with a stable schema and metadata (timestamp, host, OS, architecture). allow easy exporting (file save, clipboard) and deterministic formatting.

- Improve partial parsing UX: show parsing progress for incomplete lscpu blocks, clearly indicate missing sections (MEMORY/DISKS/DMIDECODE) and prevent silent assumptions.

- Provide a diff/compare view between snapshots: highlight changes in key metrics (frequency, cores/threads, caches, vulnerabilities); offer a quick merge or ignore-diff option.

- Strengthen privacy & security posture: ensure redaction is enforced across logs, provide an audit trail with timestamps, and offer optional encrypted storage for saved snapshots.

- Implement automatic redaction on save/export: redact sensitive fields (serials, MACs, UUIDs) by default with configurable levels (none, partial, full) and apply redaction to all outputs including clipboard copies and persistent memory stores.

- Use a structured data model + export options: store LSCPU data in a defined schema (cpu, vendor, family/model/stepping, frequency, cores/threads, caches, NUMA, virtualization, vulnerabilities, flags) and offer JSON/YAML export plus a diff view between snapshots and an option to generate a one-liner pc-info from the model.

- Harden vulnerability parsing and normalization: normalize vulnerability entries to a canonical set, track status (Not affected / Mitigation / Vulnerable), attach mitigation notes and source lines, and alert if a line appears unsupported or ambiguous.

- Provide actionable, concise UX prompts: replace open-ended prompts with numbered quick actions and suggested next steps (e.g., 1) Save redacted snapshot, 2) Continue parsing additional sections, 3) Generate pc-info one-liner); allow easy continuation by pasting more data.

- Add integrity checks and anomaly alerts: run post-parse validations (e.g., consistency between logical CPUs, cores/socket, online ranges) and warn with brief remediation suggestions if anomalies are detected.

- Add a structured, privacy-first export: emit a versioned JSON snapshot with per-field redaction controls, plus a redaction-preview before saving. Auto-redact PII (serials, MACs, UUIDs) by default; allow per-field toggles and persistent memory of redaction settings.

- Persist state and show diffs between runs: store snapshots long-term and automatically compute diffs (CPU/cores, memory, disks, vulnerabilities, mounts). Present a concise “changes since last snapshot” view to surface drift or new issues.

- Harden and normalize parsing: build robust parsers for lsblk, dmidecode, and pc-info one-liners; normalize units (GiB/MiB), deduplicate devices (loop, snap, nvme), and handle partial/missing fields with clear confidence flags.

- Streamline user flow with actionable defaults: after parsing, offer a single, concise action set (e.g., Save snapshot, Export JSON, Show diff) with a recommended default workflow to minimize prompts and clicks.

- Strengthen error handling and privacy safeguards: detect data anomalies (inconsistent memory/CPU data, questionable vulnerability statuses), retry transient command failures, and clearly warn when data cannot be fully parsed or redacted; fail safe with partial outputs and audit-friendly logs.

- Auto-redact sensitive identifiers everywhere: implement automatic redaction for serials, MACs, UUIDs, and other PII in all saved snapshots and on-screen logs, with a user-tizable redaction level and an audit trail of what was redacted.

- Versioned, secure persistence for snapshots: save PC snapshots to a versioned store (timestamped JSON), optionally encrypted, with commands to list, diff, restore, and prune old entries.

- Normalize and deduplicate disk state parsing: produce a canonical, JSON-friendly disk model (deduplicated entries, stable ordering, full mapping of loop/nvme devices to mountpoints), and prevent unbounded growth from repeated “DISKS” lines.

- Simplify and harden the next-step UX: replace multiple ad-hoc options with a single recommended action plus an “advanced” path; provide a short rationale and an option to suppress future prompts.

- Strengthen parsing validation and feedback: validate each pasted DISKS line against a schema (NAME, SIZE, TYPE, MOUNTPOINT), return actionable errors with suggested corrections, and require explicit confirmation before mutating stored state.

- Enforce schema-driven parsing and normalization for disk data (NAME, SIZE, TYPE, MOUNTPOINT, etc.), with strict validation and clear warnings for unknown fields; don’t mutate on parse errors.

- Implement deduplication and reconciliation: merge new DISKS entries with the existing snapshot, assign stable IDs, and detect/prune removed devices to keep the snapshot accurate over time.

- Default privacy hardening: automatically redact sensitive fields (serials, MACs, UUIDs) in all outputs and stored data; expose a configurable toggle to disable redaction only if explicitly required.

- Add explicit persistence/export controls: commands to save the current PC snapshot to persistent memory, and to export/load snapshots (e.g., JSON) with versioning and integrity checks.

- Improve automation-friendly UX: provide non-interactive modes and machine-friendly output (JSON), with clear diff-only reporting for changes and an option to print a concise summary (counts, new vs existing) without verbose logs.

- Add a robust, schema-based parser per snapshot section (CPU, MEMORY, DISKS, FILESYSTEM) with strict validation and normalization, handling irregular whitespace, optional fields, and varying unit formats; export as structured JSON internally.

- Provide a differential view: automatically compute and display changes since the last snapshot (new/removed devices, size/usage changes, mountpoint updates) with a concise, colorized diff.

- Implement automatic redaction/privacy controls: detect and mask sensitive identifiers (Serials, MACs, UUIDs) by default, with a configurable level and an option to review before persisting.

- Enforce deterministic persistence: offer a single-command save-to-persistent memory workflow with idempotent updates, and support exporting/importing snapshots (JSON/YAML) with optional encryption.

- Improve next-step UX: propose a single recommended action and a short confirmation prompt; add a batch/auto-run mode to execute and parse multiple commands (e.g., lsblk + df -h) and update snapshots without repeated prompts.

- Add structured, versioned snapshot model with mergeable diffs: store PC snapshot, DMIDECODE, and DMIDECODE-native data as versioned objects and support safe “merge” vs. “overwrite” when new lines arrive. This enables reliable incremental updates and conflict resolution.

- Implement privacy-first persistence and redaction controls: automatically redact or mask sensitive fields (serial numbers, UUIDs, MACs) by default; expose per-field and per-snapshot privacy templates; offer a one-click “Persist with redaction” action and an explicit purge/remove option.

- Strengthen DMIDECODE parsing workflow: support streaming DMIDECODE data, validate syntax as it arrives, and provide a clear merge plan into the existing DMIDECODE section with a conflict-resolution prompt if duplicates exist.

- Add automatic data validation and anomaly checks: cross-validate related sections (e.g., memory totals from MEMORY vs df -h) and flag inconsistencies with actionable remediation notes; provide a summary risk score for quick triage.

- Improve UX for next steps and automation hooks: present 1–2 prioritized actions (e.g., “Save snapshot to persistent memory” or “Merge new DMIDECODE lines”) with one-click execution; allow enabling periodic automatic snapshots and generate audit logs for saved states.

- Automate DMIDECODE integration with a safe default: automatically merge new DMIDECODE lines into the current snapshot, but show a concise diff preview and offer per-field conflict resolution before applying.

- Enforce configurable redaction and sanitized exports: add a per-field redaction policy (none/partial/full) with a preview of what will be redacted and an option to export a fully sanitized JSON snapshot.

- Add structured parsing, validation, and merge rules: implement a robust DMIDECODE parser that validates key fields (Manufacturer, Product, Serial, UUID), flags missing/ambiguous data, and resolves conflicts deterministically or via user choice.

- Introduce snapshot versioning with diffing and rollback: automatically timestamp and version each snapshot, provide a diff view of changes, and support rollback or export/import of snapshot JSON.

- Improve the user workflow and prompts: replace multi-option prompts with a guided flow (summary -> preview -> confirm) and expose a quick “save sanitized snapshot now” command, plus keyboard-friendly shortcuts for common actions.

- Add automatic redaction with configurable rules: detect and redact serial numbers, MAC addresses, UUIDs, and other PII by default, with an option to tailor patterns and to apply redaction before any persistence or export.

- Implement incremental/partial data merging and conflict handling: allow adding new blocks (e.g., lspci, dmidecode) to an existing snapshot without overwriting unrelated fields; surface conflicts clearly and prompt for resolution or automatic policy (overwrite/keep).

- Introduce explicit snapshot versioning and provenance: timestamped snapshots with source metadata (commands run, user, sudo where applicable) and a changelog; support safe merges from file or clipboard and easy rollback.

- Provide a transparent “diff and commit” flow: show a diff of changes before saving to persistent memory; offer a confirm prompt or an automatic-save-with-backup option; constrain persistence to a clearly defined subset of fields to avoid drift.

- Improve dependency guidance and fallback paths: detect missing tools (lspci, dmidecode, lshw, etc.), suggest exact install commands per distro, and offer a safe full-gather script as a fallback with a dry-run option to minimize user friction.

- Automate GPU data collection and parsing: run the recommended commands (lspci -nnk -s 0a:00.0, lsmod, lshw -c display, dmesg with amdgpu/radeon/drm, glxinfo, vulkaninfo) automatically after snapshot and populate the GPU block without requiring manual paste; fail gracefully if a tool is missing.

- Use structured, exportable data with clear provenance: store GPU details in a machine-readable format (JSON/YAML) with stable field names (PCIAddress, Vendor, Device, Driver, Modules, OpenGL/Renderer, Vulkan) and include the raw command outputs as an optional annex for auditing.

- Strengthen privacy controls: keep default redaction of sensitive identifiers (serials, UUIDs); expose per-field or per-snapshot toggles to reveal redacted values only with explicit user consent; ensure redacted data cannot be inferred by the assistant.

- Improve resilience and guidance when tools are missing: detect absent utilities and automatically suggest Debian/apt commands to install them (and offer sane fallback data); avoid blocking the snapshot flow while providing clear remediation steps.

- Enhance UX with progress, versioning, and drift detection: show a small progress indicator for the GPU data-gathering phase, associate a versioned snapshot ID, and compute a hash/summary to detect drift between runs; offer a diff view against the previous GPU block for quick auditing.

- Add an automated GPU enrichment batch: after amdgpu is detected, run modinfo amdgpu, lspci -nnk -s 0a:00.0, sudo lshw -c display, dmesg | egrep 'amdgpu|drm|radeon' | tail -n 200, glxinfo, and vulkaninfo in one go, then merge results into the GPU block with a single progress update and final summary.

- Return structured, machine-friendly output: emit a stable JSON/YAML blob alongside the human-readable report (e.g., module_version, driver_name, apiVersion, renderer, vendor, device, memSize). Allow exporting as a non-human-readable artifact for tooling.

- Improve error handling with actionable guidance: if any command fails or a tool is missing, report the failure clearly and suggest concrete fixes (e.g., apt install pciutils mesa-utils vulkan-tools; run with sudo; check permissions) and continue collecting other data.

- Strengthen privacy controls and auditing: keep default redaction, but provide per-field toggle and a quick “export full (unredacted) snapshot” option with a clear prompt; attach a timestamped audit trail of which data was collected.

- Reduce friction and improve UX: cache results to avoid re-running identical checks, auto-run the essential GPU checks when a GPU is present unless the user cancels, and present a concise delta against the previous snapshot to highlight changes.

- Define a fixed, versioned JSON data model for GPU info (PCI, vendor, product, driver, memory, kernel modules, etc.) with timestamps and provenance. This enables deterministic parsing, easier diffs, and cross-tool compatibility.

- Implement default privacy redaction and a per-session toggle: automatically redact sensitive fields (PCI addresses, subsystem IDs, serials) unless the user explicitly opts in to reveal them; clearly indicate redacted fields in the report.

- Add a single “collect_all” workflow: batch run recommended data sources (modinfo for amdgpu and peers, dmesg DRM logs, lsmod, glxinfo/vulkaninfo, lspci) in one go, with progress feedback, error handling, and a final unified summary.

- Improve persistence with diffs and dedup: store a history of runs, show a delta since the last save, and normalize module entries to avoid duplicates; provide a clear “mark complete” or “append” action.

- Enhance UX with actionable next steps and automated guidance: present a concise, one-click set of recommended commands for missing data (modinfo, dmesg, lspci, glxinfo, vulkaninfo), and include clear hints for permission issues (e.g., when to use sudo) and how to re-run with redaction preferences.

- Auto-suggest a single, justified next action (with a brief rationale) and offer a one-click “batch run” mode to collect all relevant diagnostics in one go. This speeds triage and reduces back-and-forth.

- Enforce privacy by default: redact PCI/subsystem IDs in saved logs/artifacts, with a per-session toggle and an explicit policy explanation. Make redaction automatic unless the user opts in to full identifiers.

- Return both human-friendly and machine-readable outputs: provide a concise narrative summary plus a structured format (JSON/YAML) of all collected data (modules, dmesg snippets, hardware details, firmware status).

- Provide proactive remediation guidance: after data collection, surface likely issues (e.g., missing firmware, driver mismatch) and offer one-click remediation commands or links to fix them.

- Automate diagnostics orchestration and visibility: run a defined set of commands (lsmod/modinfo, dmesg filter, lspci/lshw, glxinfo/vulkaninfo) in a deterministic sequence, show progress, and allow pausing/canceling if needed.

- Auto-redaction by default: add a built-in redaction toggle that masks PCI/subsystem IDs, serials, and other identifiers in all saved/sharable outputs. Provide per-field controls and a one-click option (--redact) to enforce privacy.

- Structured, incremental diagnostics: emit a machine-readable report (JSON/YAML) after each data-collection step (hardware, modules, dmesg, user-space tools) plus a final human-readable summary. Include timestamps and a labeled GPU entry to ease downstream automation.

- Deterministic log gathering: replace ad-hoc prompts with a standard, bounded log-collection plan (e.g., dmesg filtered for amdgpu/drm/firmware, last N lines, with optional --full to extend). Produce consistent output sizes and avoid repetitive user prompts.

- One-shot, scriptable workflow: introduce a non-interactive command (e.g., gpu-diagnostic --full) that runs all recommended steps, outputs both human and machine-friendly formats, and writes artifacts to a specified directory or stdout.

- Missing-tools handling and guidance: detect absent utilities (lsmod, modinfo, lspci, etc.), report clearly, and offer safe install guidance or alternatives. Ensure the UX gracefully degrades rather than failing, with explicit next-action suggestions.

- Add a structured, machine-readable summary (JSON) alongside the human-readable report, capturing key fields (PCI addr, vendor/device, VRAM, BAR size, MMIO, kernel driver, firmware/VBIOS, IP blocks, resources). This enables automated checks and diffs across runs.

- Implement configurable redaction by default and per-export options (mask PCI IDs, subsystem IDs, serials). Ensure redaction is applied consistently to all outputs and logs unless the user explicitly overrides.

- Auto-detect and flag potential issues with actionable guidance (e.g., VRAM vs BAR sizing anomalies, unfamiliar/obsolete IP blocks, firmware version mismatches) and present recommended next steps with exact commands.

- Introduce a quick-check command (e.g., gpu-analyze or --quick) that prints a compact metrics set and status (VRAM, BAR, driver, ReBAR status if detectable) for rapid sharing or bug reports.

- Enable snapshot diffing and export: store multiple runs, show differences (e.g., IP blocks added/removed, firmware changes, memory mappings), and provide a diff-friendly export format to track regressions or progress over time.

- Add built-in redaction controls for sensitive identifiers (e.g., PCI bus/dev IDs, serials, subsystem IDs). Provide an easy toggle or command (e.g., redact --pci) to mask them consistently in saved logs or outputs.

- Deliver multi-level output: a concise summary plus expandable sections for details. Include a short “What to check next / actionable steps” section with exact commands, so users can act quickly without parsing the full dump.

- Auto-suggest remediation for common firmware gaps: when optional firmware/ras ta is missing, auto-generate OS-specific upgrade commands (e.g., apt/yum/dnf/pacman) to update linux-firmware and verify presence, plus a quick reboot note.

- Integrate log-context retrieval: offer a single command to fetch nearby dmesg lines around detected items (e.g., GTT faults, RAS messages) and display with timestamps, so users don’t need to request extra logs manually.

- Implement basic sanity checks and risk tagging: flag potential inconsistencies (e.g., large GTT vs VRAM values) and categorize items by severity (info/warn/critical) with corresponding recommended actions to reduce noise and highlight truly actionable issues.

- Introduce a structured diagnostic output by default: in addition to a human-friendly summary, emit a machine-readable block (JSON/YAML) with key fields (GPU model, VRAM, GART size, KFD node count, /dev/kfd presence, DMUB/VCN firmware status, dmesg hints). Include a simple health rating (OK/WARN/ERR) and actionable next steps.

- Auto-validate KFD topology against hardware: if KFD node count does not align with the number of GPUs or expected virtualization, flag a warning and auto-suggest targeted checks (e.g., /sys/class/kfd topology, rocminfo/clinfo) with one-line commands.

- Provide ready-to-run command blocks for follow-up checks: when users request diagnostic steps, respond with concise, copy-paste command blocks (no prose fluff) and brief rationale for each command.

- Add a privacy/redaction option for log sharing: implement a toggle that redacts sensitive data (PCIe addresses, host paths) by default in shared reports; clearly warn users what will be shared if they disable redaction.

- Offer lightweight live/monitoring aids: provide an optional “watch/monitor” mode to tail relevant logs (dmesg, amdgpu/kfd entries) for a short window and highlight new warnings or errors, aiding rapid triage without leaving the CLI.

- Implement a privacy filter: automatically redact sensitive data (PCI IDs, memory/VM addresses, MMIO/IO addresses) in all outputs; expose a user-toggle to disable redaction if needed.

- Deliver structured diagnostics: always pair human-friendly summaries with a machine-readable payload (e.g., JSON) containing device, memory, firmware, notable issues, and a prioritized action list.

- Provide an explicit, prioritized remediation checklist: for each finding, include exact commands, expected outcomes, and caveats; keep to a short list (3–5 items) per report.

- Improve log-scoping for dmesg pulls: auto-suggest/auto-run lateral scans that show only relevant segments around warnings/errors, then offer the full dump as an optional follow-up; highlight suspicious lines.

- Add risk/impact tagging and confidence: annotate conclusions as benign, warning, or error with a short rationale and a confidence score; include “what to monitor” and potential next steps.

- Provide structured, machine-friendly output in addition to human text (e.g., a stable JSON/YAML schema with sections for PCI, memory, MMIO, driver/firmware, notes). This accelerates automation and testing.

- Add automatic anomaly detection with a confidence score and concise risk guidance (e.g., flag unusually large GART backing, missing optional firmware, or atypical DMUB/VCN versions) plus a one-line impact assessment.

- Always include explicit, actionable follow-up steps tailored to the data (a "What to run next" block with exact commands and expected results, like dmesg grep, lspci, or sysfs checks).

- Support configurable verbosity and format (user-select concise vs. detailed; output as text, JSON, or YAML; option to export to a file or copy to clipboard).

- Enhance privacy/safety by offering redaction of sensitive identifiers (memory addresses, exact PCI subsystems) by default, with an opt-in to reveal full data for debugging.

- Add a verbosity toggle and enforce a concise default: return a short, actionable summary first, with an option to expand to detailed diagnostics only if the user requests it.

- Provide a structured, machine-friendly summary alongside natural language: include fields like device, driver, firmware, observed message, severity, and recommended actions (e.g., issue_status, confidence).

- Attach a confidence-scored, prioritized troubleshooting plan: label each diagnostic item with a confidence level (low/med/high) and a short, ordered set of actions to take next.

- Include ready-to-run data-collection commands: supply exact commands to gather relevant logs and state (e.g., dmesg around the line, amdgpu/drm info, and compositor logs) in plain text, copy-paste friendly.

- Avoid noise and repetition; deduplicate benign messages and offer a one-line “bottom line” verdict with an optional expansion path if the user sees repeated issues or performance impact.

- Provide structured, machine-readable output alongside the human summary: return a JSON/YAML blob with clearly typed fields (device_id, vendor, memory, GART backing, firmware versions, driver, runtime_pm, display, KFD/ROCm topology, etc.) plus a human-readable section. Include generated_at and a short log_excerpt for traceability.

- Flag risks with actionable recommendations: automatically annotate high-priority items (e.g., Runtime PM disabled, GART backing heavy in system RAM, optional TA ucode missing) with a severity level and concrete next steps, including exact shell commands or config changes to verify or fix.

- Baseline comparison and delta reporting: compare current results to a known-good baseline for the same device/driver version and highlight additions, removals, or deviations (e.g., GART size or DMUB firmware differences). Present a concise delta view to speed review.

- Adjustable verbosity and targeted filtering: support presets (concise, standard, verbose) and per-section filters (e.g., show only memory/GART, firmware, or driver status). Default to concise but allow quick expansion when requested.

- Context-aware follow-ups and guidance: when user asks about a topic (e.g., OpenGL/core profile implications), proactively include a brief, relevant note in the summary and offer targeted next commands or checks (e.g., glxinfo extensions, verify driver support) and optionally fetch related logs to corroborate findings.

- Implement automatic structured parsing and a concise “Key facts” summary: convert long hardware dumps (PCI/VRAM/GART/MMIO/firmware/KFD) into a fixed schema and present both a human-friendly note and a machine-readable JSON for automation.

- Add redaction controls by default: hide sensitive addresses and internal GPU/VM addresses in the summaries, with a toggle to reveal them only if explicitly requested by the user.

- Improve Vulkan guidance workflow: when asked about Vulkan, automatically detect whether vulkaninfo data is present; if not, prompt for a minimal required block or offer exact commands to collect it (deviceName, vendorID, apiVersion, driverVersion, queue families, memory heaps, extensions).

- Run quick consistency and actionable checks: flag anomalies (e.g., GART backing vs VRAM imbalance, runtime PM disabled, suspicious or missing firmware) and provide concrete remediation steps (firmware updates, BIOS/ATOM/PSP checks, driver versions).

- Provide export and mode controls: offer one-click export of the full report to JSON/Markdown, and support configurable verbosity (short takeaways vs. full dump) to fit bug reports or debugging sessions.

- Provide a structured, machine-readable summary (JSON) in addition to human-readable text. Include interfaces, addresses, lifetimes, routes, and DNS, so downstream QA and automation can parse reliably.

- Offer a single, default command set with automatic parsing and a concise summary, plus an option to paste full raw outputs. E.g., run ip -br addr show; ip route show; cat /etc/resolv.conf; ss -tulpen by default, then present key fields.

- Make prompts context-aware and proactive. If the current output is partial (e.g., only lo block), suggest the next most informative step (paste next block or run the compact summary), instead of generic options.

- Add privacy/redaction controls by default. Allow redacting addresses, hostnames, and MACs in the visible output with an optional toggle to reveal on demand; logs should respect this by default.

- Improve session-state and progress tracking. Save parsed results after each step, provide a brief checkpoint summary, and clearly outline the next recommended action to maintain flow and reproducibility across steps.

- Enforce a privacy-first default and per-field redaction: automatically redact MAC and/or IPs by default (with a configurable toggle), and offer a secure “save encrypted” option. Ensure raw values never surface in prompts unless explicitly overridden.

- Define a canonical snapshot schema with validation: include interface (name, alias), mac, mtu, state, IPv4/IPv6 addresses, lease lifetimes, networks derived, and key routes/DNS. Normalize fields (e.g., 10.0.0.0/24) and reject incomplete or inconsistent blocks until they’re completed.

- Make memory saves atomic and versioned: attach a timestamp, support versioning, and allow diff/patch merges. Add explicit modes: “save as‑is”, “redact MAC”, “redact IP”, or “redact both”, with an auditable log.

- Improve prompts for clarity and determinism: present a fixed, numbered set of next steps (e.g., 1) save current wlp5s0 snapshot, 2) paste full compact snapshot, 3) run additional commands), reducing ambiguity and accidental data leakage.

- Strengthen partial data handling and guidance: detect missing fields (e.g., IPv6 lease lines) and prompt for the next required lines, or automatically fetch and integrate them. Offer safe auto-run options for non-destructive commands (ip route show, resolv.conf, ss) with structured paste-ready outputs.

- Add a privacy-first default and configurable redaction: automatically redact IPs (IPv4/IPv6) and MAC addresses in saved outputs; expose a toggle to save as-is or redact on demand, with a per-output/global setting.

- Enforce a stable, machine-friendly data schema: output a structured format (JSON best) for interface blocks (name, altname, flags, MTU, state, MAC, IPv4, IPv6, IPv6 link-local, data_source). Ensure missing data (e.g., no inet/inet6 yet) is explicitly represented rather than omitted.

- Improve handling of partial or missing data: gracefully handle interfaces without IPs (flag as data-pending/missing), and avoid errors or misleading "up/down" inferences; suggest follow-up commands to populate data and automatically re-scan when state changes.

- Consolidate multi-source DNS/resolver data: when user provides multiple outputs (resolv.conf, resolvectl, nmcli), reconcile into a single view, clearly indicate if a stub resolver is in use vs real upstreams, and redact sensitive DNS info per the privacy policy.

- Show actionable diffs and next steps: compute per-interface diffs between snapshots, present concise change summaries (added/removed addresses, state changes), and offer explicit next steps or commands to refresh data.

- Add automatic diagnostics and remediation hints for critical items (e.g., docker0 bridge DOWN): detect linkdown and suggest concrete actions like restarting Docker (sudo systemctl restart docker), checking docker daemon status (systemctl status docker), and verifying bridge creation (docker network ls; docker network inspect bridge).

- Enhance DNS visibility and correctness: parse and display DNS configuration (resolv.conf/systemd-resolved) and show DNS servers, search domains, and reachability; flag DNS gaps or misconfigurations in the snapshot.

- Provide a machine-readable snapshot in addition to the human-readable report: emit a structured JSON (or YAML) with interfaces, addresses, routes, DNS, and ARP/neighbor state to simplify automation and testing.
